prose.utterance: What happened to the ford by the mill in the spring flood?
prose.content: The spring floods were fierce that year—I watched the water tear through with a force I'd never seen before. When it finally receded, the ford below the mill was gone entirely, carved away as if it had never been there at all. The river found itself a new path through that stretch, left nothing but broken stone and deep channels where the crossing used to be. That's why you see everyone taking the old stone bridge now. The crossing has changed, and changed for good, I'd wager.

The leather came in from the tanner on market day though, so there's hope yet. Once those bellows are stitched and ready, the forge will roar back to life. A man like Brandt doesn't stay idle long—he'll have them mended before week's end, mark my words.

prose.content:
Old Anselm's gone bad—cracked right through, the poor thing. You'd hear it yourself if you'd been here on Shrove Tuesday: instead of that great, true voice it's had these hundred years, it makes a thin, pitiful sound, like someone's banging a kettle. The crack must run deep.

prose.utterance: Tell me all the church's news from this Lent — the bell, the vestry, the porch, everything.
prose.content:
Ah, you've caught me at a time when there's sorrows aplenty to tell. The great bell—Old Anselm—that's been the heaviest weight on my heart. Come Shrove Tuesday last, I heard her ring out and knew at once something had broken within her. The sound she makes now is thin and tinny, like striking a kettle with a spoon instead of the deep voice God gave her. A crack, substantial enough to change the very nature of her song. The founder at Caster wants ninety shillings to recast her—we'd hoped for sixty, but they've given us their word on the cost. Father Berold's out gathering alms now, going house to house for the difference.

Then there was the mice in the vestry chest. Found them before we'd time to stop them, gnawing through two of the altar cloths—good linen, both of them gone now. I shut the cat in overnight and she did her work, but there's no mending what's already eaten through.

On the brighter side, we had a pilgrim stonemason come by—Wat, his name was. Steady hands, that man. He mended the cracked step at the north porch in exchange for a night's shelter. He worked the stone the way most men work bread, and it's held firm since.

So you see—losses and small mercies mixed together, as the world tends to be.

prose.utterance: Give me the whole spring's account of the south road as you remember it.

They swing wide now through Tanner's Field to spare their wheels and axles, though the field itself is paying the price in deepened ruts. The trade follows necessity, and the land bears witness.

I've had my share of noteworthies pass through. Widow Sefa came through with two laden carts this morning, all her goods bound south for Caster where her daughter keeps house. A proper relocation, honest work. I marked it as I mark all such passages.

The writs have changed our accounting too. The Lady Day writ caught me out on first reading—I thought the new toll applied even-handed to all carts, but I read it twice through as is proper, and caught the true meaning. Laden carts now pay two pence; empty ones still a penny as before. A distinction that matters.

And then there's the forester's notice nailed to this very door, bearing the baron's seal. No oak may be felled before Michaelmas. I read those words twice, as I read all writs twice.
